title: Gastrointestinal Vascular Diseases
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the vascular diseases of the gut: veins that dilate under pressure (esophageal varices and hemorrhoids), small mucosal vessels that degenerate with age (angiodysplasia), and bowel that loses its arterial supply (mesenteric ischemia, ischemic colitis, and necrotizing enterocolitis). Each disease follows directly from vascular anatomy and simple physics: where portal and systemic veins meet, which artery supplies which segment, where collateral flow is weakest, and how wall tension rises with vessel radius. Board questions usually give the setting (cirrhosis, atrial fibrillation, aortic stenosis, a premature infant) and the character of the bleeding or pain, and ask you to name the vessel, the lesion, and the mechanism.

connections.how: Raised intrahepatic resistance in cirrhosis is the usual cause of varices, and liver failure adds the coagulopathy that makes variceal bleeding lethal.

connections.to: Arrhythmias and ischemic heart disease (CV-7, CV-18-C)
connections.how: Atrial fibrillation and mural thrombus after myocardial infarction are the main sources of emboli to the superior mesenteric artery.
High shear stress across a stenotic aortic valve destroys large von Willebrand factor multimers and links aortic stenosis to bleeding angiodysplasia.
Thrombocytopenia, clotting factor deficiency, uremic platelet dysfunction, and acquired von Willebrand defects explain why these lesions bleed more in particular patients.

connections.to: Neonatal immunology and the gut microbiota
connections.how: Necrotizing enterocolitis results from an immature mucosal barrier and innate immune response meeting abnormal bacterial colonization.

blocks.text: The portal vein, formed by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, carries about three quarters of hepatic blood flow at about 5 to 10 mmHg, and the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) is normally about 1 to 5 mmHg. Portal veins have no valves, so blood follows the pressure gradient in either direction.

Pressure equals flow times resistance, and cirrhosis raises both. Fibrosis, regenerative nodules, and loss of sinusoidal fenestrations fix resistance high, and activated stellate cells contract because the liver has too much endothelin and too little nitric oxide. Meanwhile excess nitric oxide in splanchnic arterioles increases portal inflow. Blood that cannot pass the liver turns back into collaterals where portal and systemic veins meet.

The dangerous collateral lies at the gastroesophageal junction, where the left gastric (coronary) vein, a portal tributary, connects with esophageal veins that drain to the azygos system and superior vena cava. In the distal 2 to 5 cm of the esophagus these veins lie superficially in the lamina propria and submucosa with little support, so they dilate into varices, generally once the HVPG reaches about 10 mmHg; bleeding is rare below about 12 mmHg.

blocks.title: From cirrhosis to variceal hemorrhage
steps: Fibrosis and stellate cell contraction raise intrahepatic resistance
Splanchnic vasodilation increases portal inflow
Portal pressure rises (HVPG above about 10 mmHg)
Left gastric vein flow reverses into esophageal veins
Thin-walled distal submucosal veins dilate
Wall tension exceeds wall strength and the varix ruptures
Painless massive hematemesis and hypovolemic shock
blocks.caption: Resistance and inflow both raise portal pressure; rupture depends on pressure, size, and wall thinness.

blocks.text: Large, thin-walled varices (red wale marks at endoscopy) rupture most, as the worked example shows. Rupture is painless because it is a tear of a distended vein, without inflammation, ulceration, or muscle spasm to stimulate pain fibers. It causes sudden massive hematemesis, often with melena, and hypovolemic shock.

Liver disease makes the bleeding worse and its aftermath dangerous. Splenic sequestration lowers the platelet count, and the failing liver makes too little of most clotting factors. Colonic bacteria convert the protein in swallowed blood to ammonia, so a bleed often precipitates hepatic encephalopathy. Variceal hemorrhage is a leading cause of death in cirrhosis, with a mortality of roughly 15 to 20% per episode.

blocks.title: Worked example: why large varices bleed
blocks.text: Wall tension (T) in a cylinder equals pressure (P) times radius (r), and wall stress is T divided by wall thickness. At 20 mmHg and a radius of 2 mm, T is proportional to 40. If the varix widens to 4 mm at the same pressure, T doubles to 80, and if its wall thins by half as it stretches, stress doubles again to four times the start. Dilation therefore feeds on itself, and tension falls whenever portal pressure falls, even if size is unchanged.

By contrast, a Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful retching, usually self-limited, and Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural rupture with severe chest pain and mediastinitis.

blocks.predict: Splenic vein thrombosis from pancreatitis occurs in a patient with a normal liver. Where do varices form, and is the HVPG raised?
blocks.explain: Splenic blood diverts through the short gastric veins, so isolated gastric fundal varices form; the liver is normal, so the HVPG is normal.

blocks.text: Hemorrhoids begin as normal anatomy. The upper anal canal contains three main submucosal vascular cushions (classically left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior) made of venous sinusoids with direct arteriovenous communications from branches of the superior rectal artery. Smooth muscle and connective tissue anchor them, and they seal the canal and contribute roughly 15 to 20% of resting anal pressure. The term hemorrhoid means a cushion that has enlarged and slid downward.

The pectinate (dentate) line explains why the two types behave differently. It marks the junction of the endoderm-derived hindgut and the ectoderm-derived proctodeum, so epithelium, blood supply, lymph drainage, and nerves all change there.

blocks.text: Anything that forces the cushions downward or engorges them promotes hemorrhoids. Straining at stool shears the cushions distally, and raised abdominal pressure slows venous outflow from them. A low-fiber diet produces small hard stools that need more straining, and constipation prolongs it. In pregnancy, the gravid uterus compresses pelvic veins, progesterone relaxes smooth muscle and slows colonic transit, and blood volume rises. With age, the supporting connective tissue and smooth muscle weaken, so the cushions slide more easily.

Internal hemorrhoids bleed bright red blood that streaks the stool, drips into the bowl, or appears on the paper after defecation. The blood is bright because the cushions are fed through arteriovenous communications, so it is well oxygenated. They are painless because their covering has only visceral innervation. As they enlarge they prolapse: grade I bleeds without prolapse, grade II prolapses and reduces on its own, grade III needs manual reduction, and grade IV cannot be reduced. An important exception is a prolapsed internal hemorrhoid that becomes trapped and strangulated, which hurts because it swells, becomes ischemic, and drags on sensitive anoderm.

External hemorrhoids lie under somatically innervated anoderm. They cause little trouble until a clot forms in them, producing an acutely painful, tense, bluish perianal lump that resolves over days and often leaves a skin tag.

Two distinctions are tested. First, the dilated rectal veins of portal hypertension are anorectal varices, a lesion separate from hemorrhoids, and hemorrhoid prevalence is not clearly raised in portal hypertension. Second, rectal bleeding in an older adult cannot be assumed to be hemorrhoidal, because colorectal carcinoma and angiodysplasia also bleed painlessly. An anal fissure, by contrast, is a tear in sensitive anoderm and causes sharp pain with defecation.

sections.title: Acute and chronic mesenteric ischemia and ischemic colitis

blocks.text: The celiac trunk supplies the foregut, the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) the midgut from the distal duodenum to the distal transverse colon, and the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) the hindgut to the upper rectum. Pancreaticoduodenal arcades, the marginal artery, and the rectal arteries link these territories, and the splanchnic circulation receives about a quarter of resting cardiac output, more after meals.

The mucosa is injured first. Villus tips have high metabolic demand, and because arteriole and venule run side by side, oxygen shunts across near the villus base (countercurrent exchange). Injury progresses from mucosal to mural to transmural infarction, and restored flow adds reperfusion injury from reactive oxygen species.
Acute mesenteric ischemia

Arterial embolism is the most common cause, from a left atrial thrombus in atrial fibrillation or a mural thrombus after myocardial infarction. The SMA is wide and leaves the aorta at an acute angle nearly parallel to aortic flow, so emboli enter it readily and often lodge beyond the middle colic origin, sparing the proximal jejunum. Thrombosis on ostial atherosclerosis blocks the origin and infarcts the whole midgut. Non-occlusive ischemia follows shock, heart failure, or vasoconstrictors, and mesenteric venous thrombosis (hypercoagulable states, portal hypertension) gives a slower, hemorrhagic infarct.

blocks.title: Acute embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
steps: Atrial fibrillation forms a left atrial thrombus
Embolus lodges in the SMA
Midgut mucosa becomes hypoxic; lactate rises
Severe diffuse visceral pain; abdomen still soft
Mucosal sloughing causes bloody stool
Transmural necrosis inflames parietal peritoneum: guarding, rebound
Perforation, bacterial translocation, sepsis
blocks.caption: Peritoneal signs appear only after the full wall dies, so early pain is out of proportion to the exam.

blocks.text: Pain is out of proportion to the examination because ischemic bowel first activates visceral afferents, which cause intense diffuse pain, while guarding and rebound need parietal peritoneal irritation that comes only with transmural necrosis. Anaerobic glycolysis raises lactate and causes an anion gap acidosis, but lactate rises late, so a normal value does not exclude early ischemia.
Chronic mesenteric ischemia and ischemic colitis

Chronic mesenteric ischemia is demand ischemia, the gut equivalent of stable angina. Because collaterals are rich, symptoms usually need severe atherosclerotic narrowing of at least two of the three arteries. Flow cannot rise after a meal, so pain starts about 15 to 60 minutes after eating, and patients fear food and lose weight.

Ischemic colitis, the most common form of intestinal ischemia, usually reflects low flow in older adults with vascular disease, hypotension, or recent aortic surgery. It strikes the watershed zones at the splenic flexure (SMA and IMA) and rectosigmoid junction (IMA and internal iliac), while the rectum is spared by its dual supply. Milder, crampy, left-sided pain is followed within a day by bloody diarrhea, and submucosal edema and hemorrhage give thumbprinting on imaging.

blocks.caption: Pain severity tracks how much bowel is at risk and how deep the injury goes.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading an ischemia vignette
blocks.text: A 74-year-old with an irregularly irregular pulse has sudden severe periumbilical pain, a soft, mildly tender abdomen, lactate 6 mmol/L (reference about 0.5 to 2.0), and low bicarbonate. Atrial fibrillation suggests a cardiac embolus. Periumbilical pain localizes to midgut visceral afferents, and the soft abdomen means the parietal peritoneum is not yet involved. The lactate and low bicarbonate show anaerobic metabolism with an anion gap acidosis. Gradual left-sided cramps and bloody diarrhea after hypotension would instead fit ischemic colitis.

sections.title: Angiodysplasia, Heyde syndrome, and kidney failure

blocks.text: Angiodysplasia (vascular ectasia) is an acquired, degenerative lesion of older adults, usually over 60. It consists of clusters of dilated, tortuous, thin-walled veins, venules, and capillaries in the mucosa and submucosa, lined by endothelium with little or no smooth muscle. Lesions are usually under 5 mm and multiple, and most lie in the cecum and ascending colon, though they also occur in the small bowel, where they are a leading cause of obscure bleeding in older adults.

The leading explanation is mechanical and depends on the law of Laplace. The cecum has the widest diameter in the colon, so at a given intraluminal pressure its wall tension is highest. Each contraction compresses the submucosal veins where they pass through the muscularis propria. Over years, this repeated partial obstruction dilates the submucosal veins, then the venules and capillaries that feed them, until the precapillary sphincters become incompetent and small arteriovenous communications form.

blocks.title: Formation of angiodysplasia in the right colon
steps: Wide cecal diameter gives the highest wall tension
Muscle contraction compresses veins crossing the muscularis
Repeated partial venous obstruction over years
Submucosal veins, venules, and capillaries dilate
Precapillary sphincters fail; small arteriovenous communications form
Fragile ectatic vessels bleed intermittently and painlessly
blocks.caption: Age-related, low-grade venous obstruction explains why lesions are acquired, multiple, and right-sided.

blocks.text: Because the lesion is a cluster of fragile low-pressure vessels without inflammation or a mass, bleeding is painless, intermittent, and usually slow. It may appear as occult blood with iron deficiency anemia, or as episodes of maroon or bright red blood that often stop on their own. Colonoscopy shows flat, bright red, fern-like lesions; angiography shows a vascular tuft with an early-filling, slowly emptying vein.

Heyde syndrome is the association of calcific aortic stenosis with bleeding angiodysplasia. Large von Willebrand factor (vWF) multimers are the most effective at binding platelet glycoprotein Ib under high shear. Turbulent high-velocity flow through a stenotic valve unfolds these multimers, exposing a cleavage site to the plasma protease ADAMTS13, which cuts them into smaller, less active forms. The result is an acquired von Willebrand syndrome that resembles type 2A, with loss of high molecular weight multimers. The stenosis mainly makes existing lesions bleed more, and the multimer pattern returns toward normal when the stenosis is relieved, which supports the mechanism. The clue is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border in an older adult with iron deficiency.

End-stage kidney disease is also associated with angiodysplasia. Uremic toxins impair platelet adhesion and aggregation (including vWF binding and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa function), anemia reduces the red cells that normally push platelets toward the vessel wall, and heparin is used during hemodialysis. These factors make existing lesions bleed more readily; why lesions may be more common in kidney failure is less certain.

blocks.predict: An 80-year-old with a harsh systolic murmur has recurrent iron deficiency anemia. Why would the valve lesion make a colonic lesion bleed?
blocks.explain: Shear across the stenotic valve lets ADAMTS13 cleave large vWF multimers, causing an acquired von Willebrand defect that impairs platelet adhesion at fragile ectatic vessels.

blocks.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is ischemic and inflammatory necrosis of the intestinal wall, the most common gastrointestinal emergency in neonates. Most cases occur in preterm infants, especially those of very low birth weight (under 1500 g), and onset is usually after enteral feeding begins, often in the second or third week of life. The less mature the infant, the later the onset tends to be. The terminal ileum and proximal colon are most often involved, but any segment can be.

NEC arises where an immature gut meets bacteria and feeds. The preterm intestine has weak tight junctions, a thin mucus layer, few Paneth cell defensins, slow motility that lets contents stagnate, and an abnormal, low-diversity microbiota. Preterm enterocytes express high levels of toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), so bacterial lipopolysaccharide triggers enterocyte apoptosis, poor mucosal repair, and release of inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL-6, and platelet-activating factor. Regulation of mesenteric vascular tone is also immature, and the balance tips toward vasoconstriction (more endothelin, less nitric oxide), so inflammation and low flow reinforce each other. Bacteria then invade the damaged wall.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of necrotizing enterocolitis
steps: Preterm gut: weak barrier, slow motility, abnormal flora
Enteral feeds and bacteria activate enterocyte TLR4
Enterocyte death and inflammatory cytokine release
Mesenteric vasoconstriction causes mucosal ischemia
Bacteria invade the necrotic wall and produce gas
Pneumatosis, transmural necrosis, perforation, sepsis
blocks.caption: Barrier failure, an exaggerated innate response, and ischemia drive each other forward.

blocks.text: Human milk lowers the risk compared with formula. It supplies secretory IgA, lactoferrin, growth factors such as epidermal growth factor, and oligosaccharides that favor protective bifidobacteria and dampen TLR4 signaling. In term infants, NEC is uncommon and usually follows a clear low-flow insult, such as congenital heart disease or perinatal asphyxia.

Each finding follows from the mechanism. Stasis and ileus cause feeding intolerance, increased gastric residuals, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. Mucosal sloughing produces bloody stools. Bacterial invasion and cytokine release cause systemic signs that are nonspecific in a neonate: temperature instability, apnea, bradycardia, and lethargy, with thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, and sometimes neutropenia or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Tenderness, abdominal wall redness, and a palpable mass suggest transmural necrosis or perforation.

blocks.title: Radiographic signs in necrotizing enterocolitis
rows: Bubbly or linear lucencies in the bowel wall
Gas from bacterial fermentation within the wall; the hallmark of NEC
Intramural gas has entered mesenteric and portal veins; more extensive disease
Free air, outlining both sides of the bowel wall or the falciform ligament
Same loop unchanged on serial films
blocks.caption: Severity is often staged from suspected disease, to definite NEC with pneumatosis, to advanced disease with shock or perforation (modified Bell staging).

blocks.text: Complications include perforation, sepsis, and later strictures (often in the colon), and extensive necrosis that requires resection can leave short bowel syndrome. NEC must be distinguished from spontaneous intestinal perforation, which affects extremely preterm infants in the first week or so, often before feeds, as an isolated perforation of the terminal ileum without pneumatosis or widespread necrosis. Midgut volvulus from malrotation, in which the bowel twists around the SMA and obstructs, causing bilious vomiting, and Hirschsprung enterocolitis are other causes of an acute abdomen in a newborn.

integration.text: Anatomy predicts every disease in this chapter. Valveless portal veins and the left gastric to azygos connection explain varices; the pectinate line, where hindgut endoderm meets proctodeal ectoderm, sorts hemorrhoids into painless and painful types; arterial territories and their weakest collaterals explain where emboli and low flow injure bowel. Physiology supplies the physics: pressure equals flow times resistance in portal hypertension, and the law of Laplace explains why wide varices rupture and why angiodysplasia favors the cecum. Countercurrent exchange in the villus explains why ischemic injury starts in the mucosa, and anaerobic glycolysis explains the lactate.

Pathology and immunology explain why these lesions become dangerous. Cirrhosis adds thrombocytopenia and factor deficiency, aortic stenosis removes the large vWF multimers that platelets need under shear, uremia impairs platelet function, and in the preterm gut an exaggerated TLR4 response to bacteria turns ischemia into transmural necrosis. The limits of this reasoning are worth remembering: lactate is a late and nonspecific marker, and the reason angiodysplasia is more common in kidney failure is not settled.

summary: Portal hypertension reverses flow through the valveless left gastric vein into esophageal veins draining to the azygos system, dilating thin distal submucosal veins into varices.
Variceal rupture is painless and massive; thrombocytopenia, low clotting factors, and ammonia from digested blood make it a leading cause of death in cirrhosis.

Internal hemorrhoids lie above the pectinate line with visceral innervation, so they bleed bright red blood painlessly and prolapse; external hemorrhoids lie below it with somatic innervation and hurt when thrombosed.
Straining, constipation, low-fiber diet, and pregnancy push the anal cushions down and engorge them; anorectal varices of portal hypertension are a separate lesion.

Acute mesenteric ischemia, most often an SMA embolus from atrial fibrillation, causes pain out of proportion to the exam because visceral pain precedes parietal peritoneal irritation; lactate rises late.
Chronic mesenteric ischemia is postprandial demand ischemia with food fear and weight loss; ischemic colitis is low-flow injury to the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid watershed zones.
Angiodysplasia forms in the wide cecum through years of intermittent venous obstruction and causes painless intermittent bleeding and iron deficiency in older adults.
In Heyde syndrome, shear across a stenotic aortic valve lets ADAMTS13 cleave large vWF multimers; uremic platelet dysfunction similarly worsens bleeding in kidney failure.

Necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants combines barrier immaturity, TLR4-driven inflammation, and mucosal ischemia with bacterial invasion, giving distension, bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis.

verify: HVPG thresholds (normal about 1 to 5 mmHg, varices at about 10 mmHg, bleeding rare below about 12 mmHg) and the mortality of a variceal bleed (about 15 to 20% per episode) vary between sources; confirm the values NABNE expects.
The share of resting anal pressure attributed to the anal cushions (about 15 to 20%) and the classic three cushion positions vary slightly between texts.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the hemorrhoid prolapse grades (I to IV); they are included here as description only.
Robbins frames hemorrhoids as portosystemic collaterals that portal hypertension can cause; confirm whether NABNE follows that or the cushion view used here.
The proportions of acute mesenteric ischemia due to embolism, thrombosis, non-occlusive ischemia, and venous thrombosis differ between series; this chapter states only that embolism is most common.

Timing of postprandial pain in chronic mesenteric ischemia (about 15 to 60 minutes after eating) and the statement that two or more vessels are usually involved are quoted differently between sources.
The mechanism of increased angiodysplasia in end-stage kidney disease is uncertain; the proposed role of low vWF in promoting abnormal angiogenesis is omitted as unsettled.
NEC incidence (often quoted as about 5 to 10% of very low birth weight infants) and typical day of onset vary by center and era; confirm figures if NABNE tests them.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the eponyms Griffiths point and Sudeck point for the colonic watershed zones; this chapter uses descriptive terms only.
